strengths: The controlled fully-seen/partially-seen paradigm and per-orientation heatmaps expose structured generalization behavior that average OoD accuracy would obscure.

The behavioral observations are tested across multiple orientation seeds, three object families, cross-category transfer settings, four architectures, five random resamplings, and several training ablations while holding dataset size fixed.

The finding that additional fully observed instances preferentially improve generalization around in-plane rotations is potentially useful to researchers studying invariance and systematic generalization; it has an identifiable audience independent of novelty or state-of-the-art performance.
The geometric model is interpretable and provides a compact descriptive account of the observed orientation patterns.
The manuscript is generally understandable, its main visualizations are informative, and it provides public code and data links.
weaknesses: Necessary: No held-out evaluation is reported for the purported predictive model. Its logistic parameters are optimized against the same per-orientation accuracies used to report Pearson correlation, and the components appear motivated by the observed heatmaps. Consequently, correlations above 0.8 establish an in-sample descriptive fit, not prediction or a general rule. The paper should evaluate fixed parameters on held-out orientations, runs, seeds, categories, or architectures, or consistently narrow the claim to post-hoc description. Baseline definitions, parameter constraints, fitted values, optimization details, and uncertainty are also missing.

Necessary: The evidence does not establish the claimed neural mechanism or directional “dissemination.” The proposed invariance score compares activation means after averaging entire orientation sets; it does not test whether a unit or population preserves its representation across individual transformations. Similar means can arise from different response patterns. Correlation between fully-seen and partially-seen scores can also follow from their shared network, orientation partition, and threshold rather than transfer of invariance.

Necessary: The mechanistic analysis contains substantial circularity and selection concerns. “Generalizable” orientations are defined using a model fitted to network accuracy, then used to demonstrate differences in accuracy and neural invariance. Only activation pairs above a global 95th-percentile threshold are retained, but retained counts and threshold sensitivity are not reported. Figure 5 supplies visual correlations without coefficients, confidence intervals, independence-aware analyses, or causal interventions. These results support an association at most; claims that shared feature detectors drive generalization, and especially that the mechanism is brain-like, must be removed or supported by independent metrics and interventions such as feature-overlap manipulations or unit ablations.

Necessary: The broad claims exceed the experimental scope. Evidence comes from centered synthetic renderings under fixed lighting, 50 instances per category, supervised instance classification, and limited architecture-condition coverage. This can support conclusions about the tested paradigm, but not that the mechanism is a general property of neural networks or largely the same as a biological recognition mechanism.

Necessary: Increasing the number of fully-seen instances simultaneously changes which and how many instances remain partially seen. Random resampling helps, but a paired design with a fixed partially-seen evaluation set and nested additions of separate fully-seen objects is needed to isolate the claimed effect of experience diversity and strengthen the dissemination interpretation.

Necessary: Statistical and methodological reporting is insufficient for several assertions. The paper uses “significantly” without inferential results; Figure 5 pools dependent points across conditions; and exact rotation sampling, cubelet resolution, rendering/preprocessing details, repetition counts for every ablation, and treatment of Euler-angle nonuniformity or singularities are not specified. Public code is valuable but does not replace a self-contained account.

Optional: After narrowing the claims, evaluation on naturalistic backgrounds, larger pretrained vision models, and equivariant architectures would improve external relevance, while population-level representational analyses and layerwise measurements would provide more informative follow-up evidence than selected units and t-SNE.

strengths: The manuscript studies a clear and interesting question for researchers in out-of-distribution generalization, equivariance, representation learning, and computational neuroscience. The controlled fully-seen/partially-seen paradigm usefully isolates generalization to unseen viewpoints. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/tmlr_2025plus--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-mn4nijga/call-a014d8a313374c42a7da4a9cd7a7904e/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The behavioral evidence is extensive within the chosen synthetic setting: three object families, several seed-orientation distributions, five random repetitions, different proportions of fully seen instances, cross-category transfer, four architectures, and pretraining, augmentation, and data-volume controls. The per-orientation heatmaps consistently reveal structured rather than uniform generalization.

Analyzing accuracy over orientation space is substantially more informative than reporting only mean OoD accuracy. The small-angle, in-plane, and silhouette decomposition offers an intuitive geometric description of the observed patterns.

The main behavioral result—that experience with more fully seen instances improves accuracy for particular unseen orientations—appears robust enough to be of independent interest. Code and generated data are linked, and the overall experimental narrative is understandable.
weaknesses: Necessary: the claimed predictive model is evaluated primarily as an in-sample fit. Its twelve logistic parameters are optimized directly against the same accuracy field on which Pearson correlation is reported; Figure S7 even explains that weights change at each number of fully seen instances. Correlations above 0.8 therefore demonstrate descriptive goodness-of-fit, not prediction from the seed orientations alone. The authors should either fix parameters using training conditions and evaluate held-out orientations, repetitions, seeds, or categories, or consistently relabel this as a post-hoc descriptive model.

Necessary: the evidence does not establish the stated mechanism or direction of “dissemination” from fully seen to partially seen objects. Figure 5 reports contemporaneous correlations within the same trained networks; shared image geometry, training dynamics, or accuracy could produce both invariance measures. No intervention, ablation of implicated units, learning-time analysis, mediation test, or direct identification of shared features establishes direction or causality. Without such evidence, the title and conclusions should frame dissemination as a hypothesis supported by association, not as what drives generalization or as compelling evidence of a brain-like mechanism.

Necessary: the neural invariance measure itself requires stronger validation. Equation 6 compares activations only after averaging over whole orientation sets, so neurons with different orientation-wise response patterns but equal means receive perfect invariance. Requiring both means to exceed a global 95th-percentile threshold can further select unusually broad, high-response units, while the retained count L and threshold sensitivity are not reported. Per-orientation or distributional similarity measures, threshold robustness, retained-unit counts, and uncertainty estimates are needed before interpreting this quantity as unit-level orientation invariance.

Necessary: the generalizable/non-generalizable partition is not an independent test. It is produced by thresholding a model fitted to network accuracy, using an arbitrary 10% threshold, and is subsequently used to demonstrate accuracy separation and structure the neural analysis. Figure S8 therefore cannot validate the partition independently. The partition should be defined on held-out data or purely from prespecified geometry, with sensitivity analyses across thresholds.

Necessary: the scope of several conclusions is too broad. All stimuli are centered synthetic renderings under fixed lighting, test instances were already encountered in seed orientations, and most comprehensive experiments use ResNet-18. The evidence supports conditional viewpoint generalization in the tested supervised instance-classification setting, not a general feature of neural networks or a close correspondence with biological recognition. These statements should be narrowed; naturalistic or foundation-model experiments would be valuable but are not required if the claims are appropriately scoped.

Optional: report numerical effect sizes and correlations with confidence intervals, account for dependence among multiple points from the same trained network, and specify rotation sampling, cubelet resolution, rendering, and validation details more completely. Several dense figures have very small labels, and typographical issues such as “Hyperparamters,” “Peason,” and “meaingfully” should also be corrected. Because the in-sample modeling and causal-mechanistic overclaims concern two advertised contributions, they are substantive claim-support issues, yielding a leaning-reject assessment despite the promising and well-supported behavioral findings.

strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/tmlr_2025plus--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-wiamxcnz/call-0c03bbadf85d4a768cd3d16dfc1397e4/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} addresses a meaningful question with a useful controlled paradigm: fully seen and partially seen instances make it possible to study transfer of orientation robustness, while pose-wise heatmaps reveal behavior hidden by aggregate OoD accuracy.

The empirical investigation is broad within its synthetic setting: three object families, four seed-orientation ranges, multiple proportions of fully seen instances, four architectures, five resampled instance splits, and controls involving ImageNet pretraining, rotation augmentation, and reduced data.

The descriptive finding is interesting and visually consistent: generalization is highly structured over orientation space, with favorable regions associated with small-angle, in-plane, and occasionally silhouette-related transformations. The supplementary results indicate that this is not merely a single-run or ResNet-specific observation.

The geometric components provide an interpretable compact description of the accuracy surfaces. Correlations above 0.8 across reported conditions are useful descriptive evidence, even though they do not yet establish genuine predictive validity.

The work has an identifiable audience spanning OoD generalization, equivariance, representation analysis, and neuroscience-inspired machine learning. The main experimental concept and qualitative findings are communicated clearly, and the code/data links improve transparency.
weaknesses: Necessary: the central mechanistic conclusion is not established. Correlations between invariance and accuracy, and between fully seen and partially seen invariance, cannot show that invariance was “disseminated” or drove generalization; both quantities may share causes such as orientation geometry, architecture, or training condition. The manuscript should either consistently frame this as an associative hypothesis or add causal evidence such as interventions on donor examples or invariant units, with matched controls.

Necessary: the invariance metric has a consequential selection bias. Equations 7–8 retain a unit-instance pair only when both orientation-set means exceed the 95th-percentile threshold. This removes many one-sided responses—the clearest evidence of non-invariance—while averaging only over pairs already active in both sets. Moreover, averaging activations over all orientations before computing similarity can hide different orientation-tuning patterns with equal means. Results need reanalysis with a gate such as activity in either set, explicit reporting of the retained fraction L, threshold sensitivity, and a metric that preserves orientation-wise responses.

Necessary: the geometric model is fitted to Ψ and apparently assessed on the same accuracy surface, so “prediction” is in-sample description. The generalizable/non-generalizable partition is then defined from this accuracy-fitted model at 40 fully seen instances, making parts of Figures 5 and S8 data-dependent and partly circular. Fit/evaluation must be separated across orientations, repetitions, or experimental conditions, or the partition must be fixed geometrically in advance; calibrated errors should accompany correlation.

Necessary: increasing the number of fully seen instances from 10 to 40 simultaneously decreases partially seen instances from 40 to 10. Thus target-set size/composition, interference from partially seen classes, and overall orientation distribution all change together. Cross-category experiments additionally permit category identity to narrow the candidate labels, changing effective chance difficulty. A control with a fixed set and number of partially seen targets while varying only fully seen donor instances is needed before attributing improvement specifically to donor-instance diversity.

Necessary: the broad claims should be narrowed to the tested regime. The evidence comes from centered, fixed-light synthetic renderings and supervised instance classification using a limited family of backbones. It does not support categorical claims that strengthening occurs “only” for in-plane orientations, that the mechanism characterizes neural networks generally, or that it is biologically brain-like without a direct biological comparison.

Necessary: important reporting details are absent or ambiguous, including image resolution and rendering procedure, train/validation/test counts, orientation sampling measure and cubelet resolution, handling of Euler-angle nonuniformity and duplicate representations on SO(3), optimizer settings beyond learning rate, logistic-parameter constraints and initialization, whether model correlations exclude in-distribution orientations, exact correlation estimates/uncertainty, and retained neural-pair counts. These are needed to assess robustness despite the linked code and data.

Optional: plot labels and supplementary panels are unusually small, several captions substitute qualitative assertions for numerical summaries, and typographical errors remain. Larger figures, tables of exact estimates, and evaluations on less controlled imagery or modern foundation models would improve usability and scope but are not prerequisites for a properly narrowed empirical paper.

The controlled fully-seen/partially-seen paradigm addresses an interesting question about viewpoint generalization.

Dense orientation-space heatmaps expose structured successes and failures that average OoD accuracy would obscure. The small-angle, in-plane, and silhouette components offer an intuitive geometric description of these patterns.

The experiments cover several seed distributions, three synthetic object families, cross-category transfer, four architectures, five random repetitions, and pretraining, augmentation, and data-size controls. Public code and data further improve reproducibility.

The association between penultimate-layer responses and orientation-dependent accuracy is potentially useful to researchers studying learned invariance, even if it does not yet establish the proposed mechanism.

The conceptual narrative and principal figures are generally understandable, and the empirical observations could interest vision, representation-learning, and computational-neuroscience audiences without needing state-of-the-art performance.
weaknesses: Necessary: The central causal claim is not supported. Correlations among accuracy, fully-seen invariance, and partially-seen invariance do not show that invariance is disseminated from fully-seen objects, that shared feature-tuned units mediate it, or that generalization is thereby “driven” by this mechanism. Shared orientation geometry and architecture can produce the correlations. The paper must either recast this as an observational hypothesis or add interventions such as a zero-fully-seen baseline, controlled addition of fully-seen instances, shared-feature manipulations, or causal unit ablations.

Necessary: The geometric model is fitted to the same per-orientation accuracy values on which its Pearson correlation is reported; no held-out orientations, runs, seeds, categories, or architectures are used. Moreover, the fitted model defines the generalizable/non-generalizable partition used downstream, making the reported separation and neural analysis partly selection-dependent. Out-of-sample evaluation with frozen parameters and thresholds is needed before calling the model predictive.

Necessary: The proposed invariance score compares activations only after averaging over large orientation regions. Equal regional means need not imply invariant tuning. Requiring both means to exceed a global 95th-percentile threshold can select different neuron-instance subsets for the two regions and inflate similarity, while the retained counts L are not reported. The paper should report coverage and threshold sensitivity and validate the conclusion with matched units and established representational or equivariance measures.

Necessary: Several claims exceed the displayed evidence. Generalization is not literally confined to 2D rotations—the paper itself identifies small-angle and silhouette effects—and increases with the number of fully-seen instances are not uniformly monotonic across all plotted conditions. Effect estimates or confidence intervals across the five runs are needed, and the claim should be narrowed to a predominant in-plane-associated increase in these experiments.

Necessary: Claims about “brain-like” mechanisms or neural networks in general are unjustified by four architectures, a partial architecture-by-dataset evaluation, no biological measurements, and centered synthetic renders under fixed lighting in an instance-classification task. These claims should be restricted to the tested networks and setting unless substantially broader evidence is added.

Necessary: Important implementation and statistical details are missing or unclear, including the orientation sampling distribution, number of cubelets, validation/test sizes, rendering and preprocessing specifications, model-fitting protocol, and the observational unit represented by points in parts of Figure 5. These omissions impede independent interpretation despite the code link.

Optional after narrowing the claims: Naturalistic backgrounds, lighting and occlusion variation, modern pretrained foundation models, and comparisons with explicitly equivariant architectures would establish how far the descriptive phenomenon extends beyond the controlled synthetic setting.

strengths: The paper studies an identifiable and useful question for researchers interested in out-of-distribution vision, equivariance, and learned representations. Its per-orientation analysis reveals structure that would be hidden by average accuracy.

The experimental program is unusually broad for a controlled synthetic study: three object families, four seed-orientation regimes, cross-category transfer, several proportions of fully seen instances, four architectures, five repetitions, and controls involving pretraining, augmentation, and dataset size.

The evidence supports a narrower descriptive finding: in these rendered instance-classification tasks, accuracy on unseen instance-orientation combinations is highly nonuniform, is strongest near seen views and along in-plane or symmetry-related transformations, and often increases as more training identities are fully observed.

The geometric decomposition into small-angle, in-plane, and silhouette-related components is interpretable, and its strong correlations provide a useful empirical summary of the observed accuracy maps.
The main paradigm and qualitative behavioral results are generally understandable, and the public code and data links improve reproducibility.
weaknesses: Acceptance-critical: The central mechanistic claim is not established. Correlations between accuracy and the proposed invariance score, and between fully seen and partially seen scores, do not show that invariance was disseminated from one set of objects to the other or that it caused generalization. Both quantities are measured in the same trained network and share orientation partitions and units. There is no intervention, unit ablation, direct measurement of shared features, or no-fully-seen control. The causal and brain-mechanism language in the title, abstract, results, and conclusion must therefore be narrowed to an exploratory association unless substantially stronger evidence is added.

Acceptance-critical: The neural analysis is partly circular and its metric has weak construct validity. Generalizable orientations are defined by thresholding a geometric model fitted to behavioral accuracy, after which that partition is used to demonstrate accuracy differences and accuracy-invariance associations. Moreover, the invariance score compares averages over entire orientation sets; two disjoint orientation-tuning patterns can have identical means and receive perfect invariance. The arbitrary 95th-percentile filter is not accompanied by selected-pair counts or sensitivity analyses. An independently defined or held-out partition, a genuinely orientation-resolved invariance measure, and robustness analyses are needed.

Acceptance-critical: The claimed predictive model is evaluated primarily as an in-sample descriptive fit. Its nonlinear parameters are optimized against the same accuracy map on which Pearson correlation is reported, and the supplement states that component weighting changes for each number of fully seen objects. Without held-out orientations, fixed parameters transferred across conditions, or adequate complexity-matched baselines, the claim that behavior can be predicted from the seed orientations is too strong.

Acceptance-critical: Increasing the number of fully seen instances simultaneously reduces the number of partially seen instances from 40 to 10 while retaining 50 total labels. Thus the target set and number of similarly underexposed distractor classes change along with the proposed source of invariance, offering an alternative explanation for increased accuracy. A convincing dissemination test should keep partially seen targets and evaluation identities fixed while adding or varying fully seen identities, ideally including a zero-fully-seen baseline.

Acceptance-critical: The paper generalizes far beyond the demonstrated regime. The experiments use centered synthetic renders, fixed lighting, three object families, instance classification, and relatively modest supervised models; no biological data are analyzed. These results cannot support claims about DNNs or neural networks in general, nor conclusions that biological mechanisms largely apply to DNNs. Such claims should be restricted to the tested setting. Broader real-image, foundation-model, or neuroscience experiments would be valuable but are optional if the claims are narrowed.

Acceptance-critical: Important reporting ambiguities impede interpretation and reproduction, including the exact rendering and camera setup, Euler-angle order, orientation sampling distribution, number of cubelets, train/validation/test sizes, domain used for model correlations, and fitting constraints or initialization. The stated 2% chance rate for 50-way classification also conflicts with the supplement's 10% rate for cross-category experiments and needs clarification. Numerical effect sizes, correlations, uncertainty intervals, and sample counts should accompany the dense plots.

Optional: The analysis could be strengthened by accounting for duplicate and nonuniform representations induced by the Euler-angle cube, correcting the claim that axis-angle representations are always unique, comparing against image-similarity and equivariant-model baselines, and improving the readability and labeling of supplementary figures.

strengths: The supplied manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/tmlr_2025plus--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-6ztxhsn0/call-abbf355e55a34473aca296e47951c9b3/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} uses per-orientation heatmaps to expose structured successes and failures that average OoD accuracy would conceal. This is potentially useful to researchers studying viewpoint robustness and learned invariance.

The controlled fully-seen/partially-seen paradigm, constant stated image budget, multiple orientation seeds, three synthetic object families, and within- and cross-category conditions provide a substantial descriptive experiment.

Results are examined across ResNet18, DenseNet121, CORnet-S, and a ViT, with pretraining, augmentation, and data-size controls. Five repeated instance splits and reported variability are also positive design choices.

The small-angle and in-plane model components are interpretable, while the public code/data links, hyperparameters, supplementary heatmaps, and generally clear exposition aid understanding and reproducibility.
weaknesses: Necessary for acceptance: The central causal and mechanistic claims are not supported. Correlations between invariance and accuracy, and between fully-seen and partially-seen invariance, do not establish that invariance is “disseminated” or drives generalization. Both quantities share networks, transformations, partitions, and training conditions. There are no unit/feature interventions, donor-instance ablations, learning-dynamics evidence, or causal mediation tests. Likewise, calling the mechanism “brain-like” is based on analogy rather than a direct comparison with neural data. These claims must be narrowed to correlational evidence consistent with the hypothesis, or supported experimentally.

Necessary for acceptance: The purported predictive model is fitted by maximizing correlation with the same accuracy heatmap on which its greater-than-0.8 correlations are reported; Figure S7 even describes reweighting components separately at each number of fully-seen instances. Consequently this is an in-sample descriptive fit, not demonstrated prediction from the training-orientation seed. Parameters should be learned on some conditions and evaluated on held-out orientations, instances, seeds, or repetitions, with appropriate spatial baselines and uncertainty.

Necessary for acceptance: The neural analysis inherits a problematic partition. “Generalizable” orientations are selected using a 10%-of-maximum threshold on a model already fitted to accuracy. Because Pearson-correlation fitting does not calibrate model values to accuracy, that threshold has no principled relationship to chance performance. Subsequent accuracy separation and invariance analyses therefore contain outcome information by construction. An independently defined, held-out criterion and threshold-sensitivity analysis are needed.

Necessary for acceptance: The proposed invariance score compares activations only after averaging across whole orientation sets. It can be high even when a unit has different orientation tuning within the two sets, and an always-active but nonselective unit can count as invariant. Maximum normalization and 95th-percentile activity filtering introduce further choices without robustness checks. Figure 5 supplies neither correlation estimates nor uncertainty/significance tests despite using terms such as “significantly”; its aggregated points are also dependent and confounded by architecture, object set, and data diversity. Stronger selectivity/representation controls and independence-aware statistics are required.

Necessary for acceptance: Increasing the fully-seen count simultaneously decreases the partially-seen target count from 40 to 10 and redraws target identities. Thus the training composition and evaluated population change together; holding the total image count constant does not isolate donor-instance diversity. A paired design with fixed partially-seen targets, or substantially narrower interpretation of this manipulation, is needed.

Necessary for acceptance: The broad scope of several conclusions exceeds the evidence. The task is instance classification of known, centered synthetic objects rendered with fixed lighting; partially-seen objects are not novel objects, only known objects in novel views. Architecture coverage is also uneven, with the ViT tested only on airplanes under one seed. Claims about unfamiliar objects, real object recognition, or “neural networks in general” should be restricted to the studied regime unless broader evidence is added.

Necessary for reproducibility and interpretation: The paper does not fully specify rotation order, sampling measure, or cubelet resolution. Uniformly sampling/discretizing Euler coordinates is not uniform on SO(3) and involves coordinate singularities or equivalent rotations, potentially biasing “all-orientation” averages and heatmaps. The sampling measure should be documented and either corrected or reflected in narrower claims. Optional improvements include numerical result tables, more legible plot labels, direct tests of in-plane versus other orientation subsets, and comparisons with equivariant models; these are useful context but are not demands for state-of-the-art performance.

strengths: The complete manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/tmlr_2025plus--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-rywkqqgv/call-63c1531ce01f406f9c6f0fd13bad79b9/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} studies a clear and relevant question: how object-instance classifiers generalize across unseen 3D orientations.

The orientation-resolved heatmaps reveal structured behavior that aggregate accuracy would obscure. The recurring small-angle and in-plane patterns are interesting and potentially useful to researchers studying equivariance, robustness, and representations.

The empirical investigation is broad for a controlled synthetic study: four orientation seeds, three object families, cross-category transfer, multiple CNN/transformer architectures, five random repetitions, and controls involving pretraining, augmentation, and dataset size.

The geometric model is interpretable, and its component ablations provide a concise descriptive account of the observed orientation patterns. The increase in OoD accuracy with additional fully seen instances is visually and quantitatively consistent across many reported settings.

The manuscript is generally clear, well organized, and supported by informative figures. Public code and generated data strengthen reproducibility, and the limitations section appropriately acknowledges the supervised setting and modest model scale.
weaknesses: Necessary: the strongest mechanistic statements exceed the evidence. Correlations among accuracy, fully seen invariance, and partially seen invariance do not establish that invariance is causally disseminated from one instance set to the other; orientation geometry or other shared causes could generate both. The paper should either describe this as an associative, hypothesis-generating result or add interventions, training-time analyses, random-network controls, or feature/unit ablations that test direction and mediation.

Necessary: the geometric model is fitted by optimizing correlation and apparently evaluated on the same orientation data. No held-out orientations, seeds, runs, or datasets—and no parameter-sharing protocol—are specified. Accordingly, “predictive” should be replaced by “descriptive fit,” unless out-of-sample evaluation is supplied. Moreover, the generalizable/non-generalizable partition is derived from this fitted model and then used to demonstrate accuracy separation and representation effects, making those analyses non-independent; the arbitrary 10% threshold also needs sensitivity analysis.

Necessary for the dissemination interpretation: increasing the number of fully seen instances while fixing the total at 50 simultaneously decreases the number of partially seen instances. Thus, the effect attributed specifically to additional fully seen experience is not isolated from the changed training composition. A matched control holding the partially seen set fixed, ideally including a zero-fully-seen baseline, would make the causal interpretation convincing.

The proposed invariance statistic compares orientation-set averages, so distinct orientation-specific response patterns can receive the same score. Its 95th-percentile activity filter may also select different neuron-instance populations across conditions, yet the retained counts and threshold sensitivity are not reported. Results with paired-orientation measures, alternative similarity metrics, multiple layers, and explicit within-group correlations would better support the representational account.

Several quantitative and reproducibility details are missing from the manuscript: test-set and cubelet sample counts, orientation-sampling distribution, rendering/preprocessing details, maximum training duration, and the exact level at which model parameters are fitted. Claims of “significantly higher” invariance lack statistical tests, effect estimates, or confidence intervals. Uniform binning in Euler coordinates also weights SO(3) non-uniformly and contains equivalent representations, so the dependence of averages and correlations on this parameterization should be discussed or controlled.

The demonstrated scope is synthetic, fixed-lighting instance classification using 50 curated shapes and mostly small networks. Claims about object recognition generally, neural networks in general, or brain-like mechanisms should be narrowed accordingly. Testing natural backgrounds, occlusion, real imagery, and larger pretrained vision models would be valuable but is optional once the present claims are properly scoped.

strengths: The fully-seen/partially-seen paradigm targets an interesting form of pose-OOD generalization, and the per-orientation heatmaps reveal structure that average accuracy would obscure.

The empirical study is unusually broad within its synthetic setting: three object families, four seed-orientation ranges, multiple proportions of fully-seen instances, five resamplings, cross-category conditions, four architectures, and pretraining, augmentation, and data-size controls. These results support the limited descriptive finding that accuracy is strongly orientation-dependent and often improves at in-plane-related orientations.

The geometry-based components provide interpretable hypotheses about small-angle, in-plane, and silhouette-related behavior. The supplement usefully separates generalizable and non-generalizable regions and reports several robustness checks.

The problem and observed behavioral patterns should interest researchers studying OOD vision, invariance, and learned representations; the contribution does not need state-of-the-art performance or a new architecture to be publishable.
The manuscript is generally organized clearly, formalizes its metrics, states the number of repetitions and major hyperparameters, and provides code and data links.
weaknesses: Necessary: The central mechanistic conclusion is not established. Figure 5 reports correlations, yet the paper repeatedly concludes that generalization is “driven by” invariance disseminated from fully-seen to partially-seen instances and calls this a brain-like mechanism. The proposed score first averages activations over entire orientation sets, so neurons with entirely different orientation-response patterns can receive perfect “invariance”; requiring both averages to exceed the 95th-percentile threshold also mechanically selects co-active pairs and pushes similarity upward. Equality of penultimate-layer activation magnitudes does not demonstrate feature selectivity, task relevance, or causal transfer. The shared geometry and shared trained network offer alternative explanations for the full/partial correlation. The claims must be narrowed to associations consistent with the hypothesis, or supported using directional controls such as zero fully-seen instances, matched training trajectories, representation or unit interventions, and tests against alternative explanations.

Necessary: The claimed predictive model is fitted and evaluated on the same accuracy map. Its four transformed components contain twelve fitted logistic parameters optimized directly for Pearson correlation with Ψ, and the larger full model is compared with lower-capacity ablations without held-out evaluation or complexity control. Thus correlations above 0.8 demonstrate an in-sample descriptive fit, not prediction from the seed orientation alone or necessity of the proposed components. Moreover, the fitted model at 40 fully-seen instances defines the “generalizable” regions later used to validate accuracy separation and neural associations, introducing outcome-dependent circularity. The model should be evaluated on held-out orientation bins, seeds, object classes, architectures, or runs; the partition should be defined independently; and raw-image-similarity, random-feature, and comparably flexible spatial baselines are needed. Otherwise, the language should be changed from predictive explanation to descriptive curve fitting.

Necessary: Increasing the number of fully-seen instances simultaneously decreases the number of partially-seen target instances because the total remains 50. This changes the evaluated population, the number of similarly distributed competing labels, and—in cross-category experiments—the effective chance level, which the supplement itself indicates can reach 10%. Keeping the total number of images fixed does not remove this confound. A causal data-diversity conclusion requires a fixed, preferably nested set of partially-seen targets while independently varying fully-seen experience, including a zero-fully-seen baseline and chance-adjusted analyses.

Necessary: Statistical support for the main representation claims is incomplete. The manuscript gives visually dense scatterplots but no numerical correlations, confidence intervals, or analyses accounting for repeated measurements and heterogeneous architectures/conditions; several heatmaps show only one repetition. Report effect sizes and uncertainty, use run- or condition-level held-out analyses, and clarify the number of observations contributing to every aggregate.

Necessary: The scope of the conclusions should match the evidence. Experiments use centered synthetic renders under fixed lighting, only three object families, and instance classification; ViT also receives substantially narrower coverage than ResNet. This does not support statements about neural networks “in general,” biological mechanisms, or realistic object recognition without qualification. The Euler-angle cube additionally does not globally preserve SO(3) proximity or uniform measure, so the sampling distribution, duplicate/singular representations, cubelet weighting, rendering details, and exact train/validation/test construction need clarification.

Optional: Experiments on textured objects, cluttered backgrounds, category-level recognition, larger foundation models, and temporally linked views would improve external relevance. Numerical summary tables, larger figure labels, and correction of typographical and notation inconsistencies would improve usability but are not the main reason for the rating.

strengths: The controlled fully-seen/partially-seen paradigm cleanly isolates transfer of orientation experience, while the orientation-wise analysis reveals structure obscured by aggregate OoD accuracy.

The empirical coverage is strong: three object families, cross-category conditions, four architectures, five resamplings, and controls involving pretraining, augmentation, and dataset size. The central behavioral phenomenon is therefore more convincing than a single-model demonstration.
The geometric model provides an interpretable summary of the observed patterns, and its component ablations help distinguish small-angle, in-plane, and silhouette-related effects.

The findings have an identifiable audience spanning OoD generalization, representation analysis, and computational neuroscience. The manuscript is generally clear, uses informative figures, formalizes its analyses, and provides code and data links.
weaknesses: Necessary: The claimed predictive model appears to be fitted and evaluated on the same orientation-accuracy data, apparently with weights refitted across conditions. Correlations above 0.8 therefore establish a compact descriptive fit, not prediction from seed orientations alone. The paper should either evaluate fixed parameters on held-out orientations, seeds, runs, or categories, or consistently narrow the claim to descriptive modeling. Because the generalizable/non-generalizable partition is subsequently derived from this accuracy-fitted model, an independent partition or sensitivity analysis is also needed to avoid partial circularity.

Necessary: The mechanistic conclusions exceed the correlational evidence. Correlations between accuracy, fully-seen invariance, and partially-seen invariance do not show that invariance was disseminated from one instance set to the other; shared orientation geometry and the common partition can produce these relationships. Nor does the small qualitative unit sample establish tuning to shared semantic features. Without interventions, training-dynamics evidence, or unit/feature ablations, claims such as "driven by," "enable," and "brain-like mechanism" should be reframed as a plausible representational hypothesis.

Necessary: The statement that increasing the number of fully-seen instances strengthens OoD generalization across conditions is stronger than Figure 4a supports: several beta-seed and especially alpha-prime-seed cases are flat or non-monotonic. Trend estimates with uncertainty should be reported, and the claim restricted to the conditions and orientation regions showing reliable increases.

Necessary: Several protocol details need clarification for interpretation and reproducibility. A 50-way classifier implies 2% chance, whereas Figure S8 additionally treats 10% as chance in cross-category settings; the candidate label set must be specified. The manuscript should also state the orientation-sampling measure, cubelet count, split sizes, and whether model parameters are shared across repetitions and conditions. Broad conclusions should remain scoped to centered, fixed-light synthetic renderings and supervised instance classification.

Optional: Report numerical correlations and confidence intervals for the neuronal analyses, analyze associations within generalizable/non-generalizable groups rather than relying on pooled scatter plots, test the 10% and 95th-percentile thresholds, show aggregate rather than single-run heatmaps, and correct the remaining typographical and notation inconsistencies.

Please evaluate the paper critically using the journal's acceptance criteria and give an overall recommendation according to the scale below.

First assess whether the claims are supported by accurate and convincing evidence. Material gaps may require additional evidence or narrower claims. Then assess whether some members of the intended research audience could learn something of interest and whether the writing communicates those findings clearly enough to understand and use them.

Do not impose a conference-style significance threshold or require a new method or state-of-the-art performance as a condition of acceptance. Distinguish the basic publication criteria from exceptional-impact certifications. Explain necessary changes separately from optional improvements, using the supplied manuscript without assuming a rebuttal or revisions that are not present.

Assign Overall Assessment (OA) using only: 1, 2, 3, or 4.
These numbers are an experimental ordinal encoding of TMLR's textual reviewer recommendations, not an official TMLR numerical score. They do not define equal distances between recommendations.

Rating scale:
1 = reject
The current work fails a required acceptance criterion in a substantive way.

2 = leaning reject
Important concerns about a required criterion remain unresolved, although the work has a plausible path toward satisfying it.

3 = leaning accept
The evidence generally supports both acceptance criteria, with limited reservations that should be stated precisely.

4 = accept
The claims are adequately supported, the findings have an identifiable interested audience, and the paper communicates them clearly enough for that audience.

strengths: The manuscript studies a clear and important question using per-orientation accuracy maps rather than only aggregate OoD accuracy, revealing interpretable small-angle and in-plane generalization structure. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/tmlr_2025plus--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-kj1od028/call-126f98d4f00b4abfa9d042da589d49e2/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The main behavioral trends are examined across three object families, cross-category transfer, four seed distributions, several architectures, five random repetitions, and controls involving pretraining, augmentation, and dataset size.

The geometric model is interpretable: its component ablations provide useful evidence that small-angle similarity dominates in some settings while in-plane rotation increasingly explains performance as full-view experience grows.

The experimental paradigm, heatmaps, and figures communicate the principal empirical phenomenon effectively. Researchers studying invariance, equivariance, and visual OoD generalization could learn something useful from these findings.
Public code and data materially improve reproducibility.
weaknesses: Necessary: The causal mechanistic claims are not established. Correlations among full-view invariance, partial-view invariance, and accuracy do not show that invariance was transferred from fully-seen objects, nor that shared feature detectors caused generalization. There is no intervention on full-view experience or feature overlap, no training-dynamics evidence, and no biological comparison supporting the repeated “brain-like mechanism” conclusion. These claims should be narrowed to representational associations and a candidate hypothesis, or supported with causal experiments.

Necessary: The geometric model is called predictive, but no held-out evaluation is reported. Its component nonlinearities are fitted directly to the measured accuracy map by optimizing Pearson correlation, after which correlation with that same map is presented. The paper should test fixed parameters on held-out orientations, repetitions, seeds, or object families; otherwise it should describe the result as an in-sample explanatory fit.

Necessary: The proposed invariance score compares activations only after averaging over entire orientation sets. Equal set means can produce a score near one even when responses vary substantially and do not match at individual orientations, so this is not by itself evidence of orientation-invariant tuning. Moreover, the 95th-percentile filter selects potentially different neuron-instance populations across conditions, but retained counts and threshold sensitivity are not reported. The metric needs validation against orientation-resolved alternatives and robustness analyses.

Necessary: Generalizable orientations are defined using a model fitted to accuracy in the 40-fully-seen condition and then reused in analyses claiming that this partition separates accuracy and invariance. This outcome is partly built into the construction and risks information leakage. The partition should be defined independently—for example, solely from preregistered geometry—or evaluated on genuinely held-out experiments.

Necessary: Increasing the number of fully-seen instances simultaneously decreases the number of partially-seen target instances and raises the fraction of training images sampled across all poses. Consequently, the experiments do not isolate object-instance diversity from pose exposure or target-set composition. A matched control is needed, or the attribution to “dissemination from an increasing number of familiar objects” must be narrowed.

Necessary: Claims about neural networks in general exceed experiments conducted on centered, fixed-light synthetic renderings in a supervised instance-classification task; most conditions use ResNet-18, while other architectures receive reduced coverage. Conclusions should be scoped to the tested regime and distinguish robustness across these models from generality to natural images, modern large vision models, or biological vision.

Optional: Report numerical effect sizes and confidence intervals, fitted-model uncertainty, retained-neuron counts, and sensitivity to the 10% partition and 95th-percentile activity thresholds. Exact orientation sampling, cube resolution, rendering settings, preprocessing, checkpoint selection, and the stated 10% chance level in cross-category experiments also need clearer documentation.

strengths: The complete manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/tmlr_2025plus--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-7ku0ira7/call-2b86459dd04e4638afca8d5ac240a1ad/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} studies an important, well-defined question and usefully maps accuracy over orientations instead of reporting only an aggregate OoD score.

The controlled experiments span three object families, four seed-orientation distributions, within- and cross-category conditions, several proportions of fully seen instances, four architectures, and five random repetitions. Pretraining, augmentation, and dataset-size controls further improve the descriptive evidence.

The results convincingly demonstrate structured pockets of above-chance recognition at unseen orientations. The geometric decomposition into small-angle, in-plane, and silhouette-related components is intuitive and potentially useful for researchers studying transformation generalization.

The figures communicate the main behavioral patterns effectively, and the released code and data improve reproducibility. The findings have an identifiable audience in OoD generalization, representation learning, and computational vision.
weaknesses: Necessary: The central mechanistic conclusion is not supported by causal evidence. Correlations among accuracy, fully seen invariance, and partially seen invariance cannot establish that invariance is transferred from fully seen objects, that shared feature-tuned units mediate performance, or that the mechanism is brain-like. Common orientation geometry can produce all three correlations. The title, abstract, and conclusions should be narrowed to an observational association unless supported by interventions, training-time analyses, feature-overlap measurements, or selective unit/representation ablations.

Necessary: The purported predictive model is developed after inspecting the heatmaps and its roughly 12 nonlinear parameters are fitted and evaluated on the same accuracy maps. Moreover, the generalizable/non-generalizable partition is derived from this accuracy-fitted model and then reused in the accuracy and neural analyses. This makes Figures 5 and S8 partly circular. Evaluation should use genuinely held-out orientations, objects, seeds, or runs, with the partition fixed without target-condition accuracy, and should compare against credible image-similarity and smooth SO(3) baselines. Pearson correlation alone also measures neither calibration nor absolute predictive accuracy.

Necessary: The invariance statistic does not adequately establish unit-level invariance. It compares means over large orientation sets, so disjoint response profiles can receive a perfect score if their means agree. Requiring both averaged activations to exceed a 95th-percentile threshold selects high-high pairs and allows different neuron-instance subsets and different counts L in each comparison, potentially inducing the observed separation. The paper should report L, retain a common population, quantify uncertainty, and test orientation-resolved or subspace-level invariance robust to representation basis.

Necessary: Increasing the number of fully seen instances from 10 to 40 simultaneously reduces partially seen test instances from 40 to 10 and changes which competing classes receive full pose coverage. Consequently, increased OoD accuracy is not uniquely attributable to additional fully seen experience or dissemination. A decisive control must hold the partially seen target set and label space fixed while independently varying the number or pose coverage of fully seen source instances, ideally including a zero-fully-seen baseline.

Necessary: The claim that gains occur "only" for in-plane rotations is inferred from increasing correlation with a fitted in-plane component, rather than a direct statistical comparison of accuracy gains inside versus outside independently defined in-plane regions. weaknesses: Necessary: The strongest mechanistic language is not supported by the presented evidence. Moreover, the invariance score compares set-averaged scalar activations, so units responding differently across individual orientations can still score as invariant. The causal claims should be narrowed to an association and hypothesis unless supported by interventions, cross-decoding, lesions, or stronger representational analyses.

Necessary: Evaluation of the explanatory model is not demonstrably out of sample. Its parameters appear to be optimized against the same per-orientation accuracies on which correlations are reported, while the generalizable/non-generalizable partition is subsequently derived from that fitted model and reused in the neural analysis. Correlation coefficients, uncertainty, and sensitivity to both partition and activation thresholds should be reported numerically.

Optional: Comparisons with image-similarity or nearest-neighbor baselines, random-feature networks, and equivariant architectures would clarify how much of the spatial pattern reflects learned neural invariance rather than visual similarity or task geometry.

Optional: Several composite plots have very small labels, and the manuscript contains minor typographical and grammatical errors. Enlarging or splitting dense figures and performing a careful copy edit would improve usability.

strengths: The paper studies a well-defined and relevant question: how recognition varies across unseen object orientations rather than only in aggregate. The per-orientation heatmaps reveal structured behavior that should interest researchers in robustness, representation learning, and computational vision.

The experimental paradigm is systematic. It varies the number of fully seen instances, four seed-orientation distributions, three object families including asymmetric objects, cross-category transfer, and multiple architectures. Five random repetitions and controls involving pretraining, augmentation, and dataset size provide useful robustness evidence.

The central descriptive finding is convincing within this synthetic instance-classification setting: increasing fully seen instance diversity improves performance on particular unseen views, especially views related to training orientations by in-plane or small-angle rotations.

The geometric model is interpretable, closely matches the observed accuracy maps across conditions, and includes component ablations that help distinguish small-angle, in-plane, and silhouette-related effects.

The manuscript is generally clear and supplies equations, informative visualizations, code, and generated data. The neural-activation analysis also offers an interesting hypothesis for subsequent causal investigation.
weaknesses: Necessary: The mechanistic conclusion is stronger than the evidence. Figure 5 establishes correlations among accuracy, an aggregate invariance score, and fully/partially seen representations; it does not show that invariance is transferred from fully seen instances, that shared features mediate this transfer, or that the identified units cause generalization. Necessary: The geometric model appears to be fitted and evaluated on the same orientation-wise accuracy data. Moreover, the generalizable/non-generalizable partition used in the neural analysis is defined from a model fitted to accuracy in the 40-fully-seen condition, making subsequent accuracy separation partly circular. Held-out evaluation across orientations, instances, repetitions, or conditions is needed for predictive claims; otherwise the model should be described as a post-hoc descriptive summary, and the neural partition should be defined independently.

Necessary: Several details needed to interpret or reproduce the quantitative results are missing or ambiguous, including the number of orientation cubelets, whether rotations are sampled uniformly on SO(3) or uniformly in Euler coordinates, rendering and image-resolution details, and optimization, initialization, and constraints for the logistic model. The stated 2% chance level for a 50-way task should also be reconciled with the unexplained 10% chance level assigned to cross-category experiments in Figure S8.

Necessary: The scope should be narrowed. The evidence concerns centered, fixed-lighting synthetic renders, known object identities, supervised instance classification, and mostly modest architectures; ViT is evaluated under fewer conditions. It does not by itself support broad statements about neural networks in general, real-world category recognition, or biological mechanisms.

Optional: Report numerical effect sizes and confidence intervals, correlations for Figure 5, sensitivity to the 10% generalizability cutoff and 95th-percentile activation threshold, and baselines using image similarity or untrained representations. A zero-fully-seen control would also help separate learned dissemination from transformation geometry already present in the inputs.

The fully-seen/partially-seen paradigm and per-orientation heatmaps reveal structured behavior that would be obscured by reporting only mean OoD accuracy.

The behavioral study is broad for a controlled experiment: it covers several orientation seeds, three object families, cross-category transfer, four architectures, five random repetitions, and pretraining, augmentation, and data-size controls.
The proposed small-angle, in-plane, and silhouette components provide an intuitive geometric vocabulary for describing the observed accuracy patterns.

The exposition and figures are generally clear, and public code and data improve reproducibility. The empirical behavioral findings would remain useful even with substantially narrower mechanistic claims.
weaknesses: Necessary: the central claim that invariance is “disseminated” through shared features and drives generalization is not established by the correlational analyses. Penultimate-layer similarity and accuracy are expected to covary, while selected top-activating examples do not identify shared causal features. There is also no direct biological comparison supporting the “brain-like mechanism” conclusion. These claims should be reframed as correlational hypotheses or supported with interventions, matched controls, and feature-level causal tests.

Necessary: the 12-parameter geometric model appears to be fitted and evaluated on the same per-orientation accuracies. Moreover, its fitted output defines the generalizable/non-generalizable partition subsequently used to demonstrate accuracy separation and representation differences. This makes the advertised prediction partly in-sample and the partition-based validation circular. Parameters and partitions should be fixed independently and evaluated on held-out orientations, seeds, object sets, architectures, or runs.

Necessary: varying the number of fully-seen instances simultaneously changes the number and composition of partially-seen training/test classes, so it does not cleanly isolate experience diversity. The manuscript also invokes both 2% and 10% chance levels without adequately explaining the applicable classifier or candidate set. A fixed partially-seen test set, an appropriate control, and an exact account of label spaces and chance levels are needed.

Necessary: the invariance score compares activations only after averaging across orientation sets, so disjoint orientation tuning can receive a high score when the means coincide. Requiring both averages to exceed a global 95th-percentile threshold can further select for high similarity, yet retained-pair counts and threshold sensitivity are not reported. Numerical correlations, uncertainty, statistical tests, and robustness to alternative representation metrics are needed before calling the differences significant.

Optional: evaluation on naturalistic backgrounds, additional categories, uniformly sampled SO(3) rotations, and larger pretrained vision models would strengthen external validity. These extensions are not required if claims are explicitly restricted to the controlled rendered instance-classification setting and the architectures actually tested.

strengths: The controlled fully-seen/partially-seen paradigm isolates transfer of orientation robustness while holding the total number of instances and training images fixed. Five random repetitions and extensive per-orientation evaluation provide substantially more evidence than aggregate accuracy alone.

The main behavioral finding is convincing: additional fully-seen instances improve generalization in structured regions of orientation space, especially in-plane rotations. This pattern recurs across multiple seeds, three object families, cross-category transfer, and several training-set sizes.

Results across ResNet-18, DenseNet-121, CORnet-S, and ViT, together with pretraining, augmentation, and data-size controls, reduce the likelihood that the phenomenon is an artifact of one architecture or training choice.
The geometric decomposition into small-angle, in-plane, and silhouette components is interpretable, and its ablations help explain which transformations account for the observed accuracy maps.

The work should interest researchers studying OOD generalization, learned invariance, vision, and neuro-inspired representation analysis. The paper is generally understandable, and releasing code and generated data supports reuse.
weaknesses: Necessary: the geometric model is called predictive, but its logistic parameters appear to be optimized against the same accuracy maps on which correlation is reported, separately for each condition. The reported correlations therefore establish an explanatory in-sample fit, not out-of-sample prediction. The authors should either evaluate fixed parameters on held-out orientations, repetitions, architectures, or categories, or narrow the predictive claims accordingly.

Necessary: the evidence for a dissemination mechanism is correlational rather than causal. The generalizable partition is itself derived from a model fitted to accuracy, and pooled correlations among accuracy, fully-seen invariance, and partially-seen invariance can arise from shared orientation geometry or experimental condition. Claims that invariance drives generalization—and especially that the mechanism is brain-like—should be framed as a supported hypothesis unless strengthened with interventions, appropriate controls, and within-condition statistics.

The invariance analysis is sensitive to design choices that are insufficiently characterized: activations are averaged across entire orientation sets before comparison, only pairs exceeding a global 95th-percentile threshold are retained, and the retained count L and threshold sensitivity are not reported. These details are needed to show that the result is not driven by selection or aggregation effects.

Some essential reporting is missing or difficult to recover from the manuscript, including the Euler-angle convention and sampling measure, number of orientation bins, complete rendering and split details, model-fitting protocol, and numerical correlation estimates with uncertainty. Uniform Euler-angle sampling is also not uniform on SO(3), so global average-accuracy claims should specify or correct the induced weighting.

Optional: validation under variable lighting, backgrounds, scale, and natural imagery would clarify external validity. The present evidence supports controlled rendered instance classification, but not broad claims about neural networks generally or biological object recognition. A zero-fully-seen control, direct image-similarity baselines, and neuron-ablation or permutation controls would also sharpen the mechanistic interpretation.

strengths: The controlled fully-seen/partially-seen paradigm and orientation-resolved analysis reveal structured OOD behavior that average accuracy would obscure. The heatmaps and aggregate results are mutually consistent in the complete manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/tmlr_2025plus--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-iuuragk4/call-10e044e1dc6445308dc371529a9ed969/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.

The behavioral phenomenon is tested across multiple pose seeds, three synthetic object families, cross-category settings, four substantially different architectures, five random repetitions, and pretraining, augmentation, and data-volume controls.

The geometric components provide an interpretable description of where generalization occurs. Their ablations connect the observed increase primarily to in-plane rotations rather than merely reporting a single aggregate accuracy.

The representation analysis uncovers a strong association among activation invariance, orientation-specific accuracy, and fully-seen versus partially-seen instances. This is an interesting finding for researchers studying learned invariance even without treating it as a causal mechanism.
The learning setup, central findings, figures, and limitations are generally communicated clearly, and both code and generated data are linked.
weaknesses: Necessary: The evidence does not establish the claimed mechanism of invariance being “disseminated” from fully-seen to partially-seen objects. Correlations between two invariance summaries from the same network can also arise from shared geometry, parameters, normalization, or selection. The paper needs a causal intervention or must consistently frame dissemination, feature tuning, and the “brain-like mechanism” as hypotheses supported by correlational evidence rather than identified mechanisms.

Necessary: The supposedly predictive geometric model is fitted and evaluated against the same per-orientation accuracies, apparently with condition-specific parameters. Its high correlation therefore demonstrates descriptive fit, not prediction of unseen behavior. Held-out orientations or experiments, transfer of fitted parameters across conditions, and uncertainty over correlations are needed; otherwise the predictive claims should be narrowed. Defining the generalizable set using this accuracy-fitted model also makes the subsequent accuracy/invariance separation partly outcome-dependent.

Necessary: Increasing the number of fully-seen instances simultaneously decreases the number of partially-seen test instances and changes the training mixture. This changes discrimination difficulty and, especially in cross-category experiments, the effective chance level. A control retaining a fixed partially-seen test cohort, or a careful chance-normalized analysis and narrower causal wording, is needed before attributing the increase specifically to instance diversity and invariance transfer.

Optional: Report numerical correlations and confidence intervals for Figure 5, the retained count L after the 95th-percentile activation filter, sensitivity to that threshold and the 10% generalizability cutoff, and analyses across layers or against untrained/permuted controls. These would make the neural evidence substantially easier to assess.

Optional: The synthetic, centered, fixed-lighting instance-classification setting supports a controlled result but not broad conclusions about neural networks or biological recognition in general. Sharper scope statements, fuller self-contained rendering and split details, and correction of several typographical errors would improve precision.

strengths: The orientation-resolved evaluation is informative: the heatmaps reveal structured successes and failures that average OoD accuracy would conceal.

The empirical study covers three object families, multiple seed-orientation distributions, cross-category transfer, four architectures, five random repetitions, and pretraining, augmentation, and data-size controls.

The small-angle, in-plane, and silhouette components provide an interpretable geometric description of the observed accuracy patterns; the reported correlations are consistently high across the tested settings.
The controlled synthetic paradigm isolates orientation while keeping lighting and framing fixed, making the basic behavioral phenomenon easy to study.
The manuscript is generally clear, includes useful supplementary visualizations, and provides code and data links.
weaknesses: Necessary: The paper's strongest mechanistic claims are not established by Figure 5. Correlations between accuracy and activation similarity, and between fully-seen and partially-seen similarity, do not show that invariance was transferred, caused generalization, or arose through shared feature detectors. The same orientation partition and network affect both axes, and there is no zero-fully-seen control, intervention, mediation analysis, neuron ablation, or comparison with an untrained network. The conclusions should be narrowed to representational associations unless causal evidence is added; the further claim of a “brain-like” mechanism is especially unsupported without a direct biological comparison.

Necessary: The manipulation attributed to the number or diversity of fully-seen objects is confounded. With 4,000 examples per instance, increasing fully-seen instances from 10 to 40 simultaneously raises the number of broadly oriented source images from 40,000 to 160,000 and reduces partially-seen target instances from 40 to 10. Constant total dataset size and the half-data ablation do not isolate source-instance diversity. The partial target set and broad-view sample budget should be held fixed, or the claim should describe this joint manipulation.

Necessary: The geometric model is fitted by optimizing correlation against the same accuracy heatmap on which its reported predictive performance is measured. Without held-out orientations, repetitions, or experimental conditions, correlations above 0.8 demonstrate descriptive fit rather than prediction. Moreover, the generalizable/non-generalizable partition used in the neural analysis is derived from this accuracy-fitted model, making the subsequent accuracy separation partly circular. Independent geometric partitions or proper train/test evaluation are needed.

Necessary: The neural metric averages activation across an entire orientation set before comparing sets and retains only pairs exceeding an arbitrary global 95th-percentile threshold. The generalizable set also uses an arbitrary 10%-of-model-maximum cutoff. No sensitivity analysis, uncertainty estimates, or controlled within-condition correlations are reported, so the apparent pooled separation may depend on these choices and on architecture or condition differences.

Necessary: Several details needed to assess the evidence are absent or unclear, including the orientation sampling distribution, cubelet resolution and sample counts, rendering/image specifications, model-fitting protocol, and effective sample sizes in the scatterplots. Uniform Euler-angle sampling would also be nonuniform and degenerate over SO(3). The 10% chance level stated for cross-category experiments is not reconciled with the described 50-way instance-classification task.

Necessary: Broad statements about neural networks in general should be restricted to supervised recognition of previously seen instances in centered, fixed-lighting synthetic renders. The experiments do not test new object instances, natural backgrounds, other nuisance factors, or modern large vision models.

Optional: Raw-pixel, nearest-neighbor, and frozen-feature image-similarity baselines would clarify whether the orientation patterns require learned invariance rather than simply tracking visual similarity. Clearer, less densely packed quantitative figures and direct reporting of correlations with confidence intervals would also improve usability.

strengths: The controlled fully-seen/partially-seen paradigm and per-orientation heatmaps reveal an interesting, structured phenomenon that average OoD accuracy would obscure: generalization concentrates around nearby and in-plane rotations.

The behavioral result is tested across four seed-orientation regimes, three object families, cross-category transfer, five instance resamplings, several architectures, and controls involving pretraining, augmentation, and reduced data. This is unusually broad evidence for a controlled synthetic study.

The geometric components of the orientation model are interpretable, and their ablations help identify in-plane rotation as the component most associated with increased generalization as fully-seen diversity grows.

The paper addresses questions relevant to researchers studying OoD generalization, equivariance, and learned representations. The main paradigm and qualitative findings are communicated clearly, with useful visualizations and public code/data.
weaknesses: Necessary: The claimed predictive result is evaluated in-sample. Twelve logistic parameters are optimized against the same per-orientation accuracy field used to report Pearson correlation, apparently separately for each experimental condition. Without held-out orientations or transfer of fitted parameters across seeds, datasets, architectures, or repetitions, the model is an informative descriptive fit rather than evidence that behavior can be predicted from the seed alone. Cross-validation or narrower terminology is required.

Necessary: The evidence does not establish the proposed mechanism or the direction of “dissemination.” Correlation between accuracy and invariance, and between fully-seen and partially-seen invariance, is compatible with both quantities responding to common factors. Moreover, the generalizable/non-generalizable partition is obtained from a model fitted to accuracy, making subsequent accuracy and neural comparisons partly circular. A causal intervention, training-time analysis, appropriately independent partition, or substantial narrowing to a correlational hypothesis is needed.

Necessary: Important details of the neural metric are insufficiently validated. Averaging activation over entire orientation regions before computing invariance can hide orientation-specific differences, while retaining only pairs whose two averages exceed a global 95th-percentile threshold can mechanically favor similar, high responses. The paper does not report the retained counts, threshold sensitivity, shuffled controls, or treatment of potentially signed ViT activations. These omissions weaken the neuronal conclusions.

Necessary: The stated partition rule appears internally unclear: orientations exceeding 10% of the maximum fitted score are labeled generalizable, yet Figure S9 shows fitted scores roughly between 1.8 and 2.4, for which that literal rule would seemingly label every displayed orientation generalizable. The implementation, calibration, and sensitivity of this consequential threshold must be reconciled.

Necessary: Claims about generic DNN and brain-like mechanisms exceed the demonstrated scope. Experiments use instance classification of 50 clean, centered CAD objects under fixed rendering conditions; transformer coverage is also much narrower than ResNet coverage. Conclusions should be restricted to this controlled regime unless supported on more naturalistic tasks and data.

The manuscript omits or leaves ambiguous several reproducibility and inferential details, including the number of orientation cubelets, the precise Euler rotation convention and sampling measure, split sizes, constraints and initialization for the fitted logistic functions, definitions of null models, and quantitative uncertainty for the Figure 5 relationships. Uniform Euler-grid averaging also does not correspond to uniform weighting on SO(3).

Optional improvements include evaluating held-out real-image or variable-rendering conditions, comparing explicitly equivariant models, using Haar-uniform orientation sampling or weighting, and perturbing or ablating identified units to test their functional role.
